item.title: Roman Series: NASA’s New View of the Dark Universe
item.description: 【节目】NASA's Curious Universe 【主题】science-space 【形态】audio, text 【生产形态】full-episode, text-script 【摘要】以 Nancy Grace Roman 的生平开场（从被劝阻学数学的女生到 NASA 首任天文主管、推动哈勃上天，被称为“哈勃之母”），再讲 Roman 望远镜本身：视场是哈勃 100 倍、巡天速度约 1000 倍，将观测逾 10 亿个星系、编目数千颗系外行星；核心科学是暗能量之谜——宇宙膨胀在加速（Alina Kiessling 的抛球比喻），Roman 将用超新星、引力透镜与原初声波印记做三维宇宙图，检验暗能量是否随时间变化；OpenUniverse 超算模拟宇宙先行排练；结尾落到“发现机器”：20 亿个星系中必有百万分之一的意外。 【Reels 角度】先给“视场 100 倍、巡天速度约 1000 倍”的体量，再用抛球比喻讲清暗能量（本以为会减速回落，结果越胀越快），最后落到 20 亿个星系里的意外发现。 【许可证】Public domain：美国联邦政府作品（NASA 官方播客），一般不受版权保护 【权利说明】可剪辑/再分发，不得暗示 NASA 背书；本集文字稿中标有音乐 cue（Curiosity 主题曲、New Development、Great Expectations、Social Progress、Goals and Objectives、Scientific Progress、A Delicate Machine、Machines Made This、Pressurization Trailer、Tentative Surge、Gene Sequencing、Ancient Starlight、Beyond Our Imagination、Points of Light），正式发布前需逐项再核片段内音乐；本批 ready-clip 已核为原声讲话段、未加 BGM。 【来源】https://www.nasa.gov/podcasts/curious-universe/roman-series-nasas-new-view-of-the-dark-universe/ 【采集日（北京时间）】2026-10-29 【发布时间精度】exact（NASA Curious Universe Megaphone RSS: Tue, 11 Aug 2026 13:08:00 -0000） 【子片段 GUID】urn:podcast:nasa.gov:curious-universe:roman-dark-universe:clip:ball:1363.9-1401.8
item.content:encoded:
[Music: Curiosity by SYSTEM Sounds]
HOST PADI BOYD: You’re listening to NASA’s Curious Universe. I’m Padi Boyd.
HOST JACOB PINTER: And I’m Jacob Pinter. NASA is launching a new space telescope that will change the way we see the universe. It’s called the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
PADI: Roman will study some of the biggest mysteries out there, answering questions about how the universe has changed over time, what’s driving its expansion, and the worlds that exist beyond our solar system. Roman has a unique ability to survey vast areas of space with incredible speed and detail. It will collect huge amounts of data, including more than a billion galaxies, and help discover thousands of planets orbiting distant stars. Roman will join other space telescopes, including Hubble and Webb. It builds on NASA’s technology and know-how that have shaped our view of the cosmos for decades.
[Music: New Development by Frederic Sans]
JACOB: In this episode: what Roman will see with its wide view of the universe. We’ll dive into dark energy, which is a huge puzzle for scientists. Roman is designed to look for answers. And we’ll meet the woman who literally got NASA astronomy off the ground. Now her name is on NASA’s new telescope.
At first, the Roman Space Telescope was not named “Roman”. It had a different name: WFIRST, an acronym for Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope, which basically describes what it can do. In 2020, NASA officials announced that it was getting a new name.
THOMAS ZURBUCHEN (Former Associate Administrator, NASA Science Mission Directorate): The person we want to rename this after is a person who had huge influence in all of astronomy and space. It's a person who imagined the influence of space astronomy before others even thought that that's possible. And that's why today I'm so excited that we can rename this telescope, for it to become the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
To set the stage for Roman, the telescope, we’re going to spend some time learning about Nancy Grace Roman, the person.
INTERVIEWER: This oral history is being conducted with Dr. Nancy Roman in her home in Chevy Chase, Maryland ... (fades out)
PADI: She was a trailblazer. She joined NASA at the ground floor, at the very beginning. And for decades, she worked behind the scenes to make the Hubble Space Telescope a reality and to show us the universe in ways we had never seen it before.
INTERVIEWER: You’ve had such a distinguished career with NASA. We want to hear about all those times and experiences that you’ve had. But we’d like to start today by you providing us some of your background and how you got started.
NANCY GRACE ROMAN: OK. To start with, I’m trying to use my double name again, Nancy Grace. I will answer either way, and I have to admit most people don’t use it. But I’m trying.
[Music: Great Expectations by Brice Davoli]
PADI: Nancy Grace Roman was born in 1925. When she was growing up, her family moved around. In Michigan she saw the northern lights. At their house in Nevada, Roman learned constellations from her mother.
ROMAN: We were the last house on the street. There were no houses across from us, an empty lot behind us, a ranch on the other side of us. So we had a really clear, dark sky, and I wouldn’t be surprised if that had a major influence on my being interested in astronomy. I don’t really know when I started. Most kids, or at least many kids, are interested in astronomy at the age of, oh, 11 or 12, and I just never outgrew it. It was as simple as that.
PADI: When Roman was going to school in the 1930s and ‘40s, there were not many women in astronomy. Plenty of people told her she shouldn’t even bother.
JACOB: In high school, Roman took Latin for years. Going into her senior year, she told her guidance counselor that she wanted to add algebra and skip a fifth year of Latin. And she never forgot the counselor’s reaction.
ROMAN: And the guidance counselor looked at me. My memory of—visions of her, I’m sure is exaggerated, but she seemed about ten feet tall, looked down her nose at me. “What lady would take mathematics instead of Latin?” which was about as obvious as you could get. [Laughter]
PADI: But Roman took algebra and kept taking math. She earned a bachelor’s degree, a Ph.D., and then a research position at a famous observatory. And it was not always easy. Even when her professors or colleagues had a kind word for Roman, sometimes it came as a backhand compliment.
ROMAN: The first encouragement that I got was in my junior year at college when the head of the physics department came up to me in lab one day and said, “You know, I usually try to talk women out of going into physics, but I think maybe you might make it.” That was my first encouragement.
JACOB: In her first job, which was part of a university physics department, Roman learned the men she worked with made more money than she did—a lot more. She also didn’t think she would get tenure, so she left.
PADI: She joined the government as an astronomer at the Naval Research Laboratory, and Nancy Grace Roman’s hard work began to pay off. Her research on a particular kind of star caught the attention of scientists around the world.
JACOB: Many years later, an interviewer asked Roman if being stubborn kept her going.
INTERVIEWER: Would you have considered yourself stubborn, and that's why you just kept persevering, or ... ?
ROMAN: Yes. I think if I hadn't been stubborn, I'd been talked out of it years earlier.
[Music: Social Progress by Brice Davoli]
JACOB: A few years later, a new door opened.
NARRATOR OF “25 YEARS OF PROGRESS”: The Space Act is signed into law by President Eisenhower on July 29, 1958, and on October 1, 1958, NASA comes into being.
PADI: The U.S. government wanted to explore space, so it created the National Aeronautics and Space Administration: NASA.
UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: They simply said that we were to pursue the development of activities in space for the benefit of all mankind.
JACOB: Now, you know what came next.
PADI: Moon landings. Space telescopes. Rovers on Mars.
JACOB: But try to imagine what it felt like to be there at the very beginning. There was an office, a big dream, and a whole lot of work to do.
PADI: A former colleague asked Nancy Grace Roman if she would be interested in creating NASA’s astronomy program. She wasn’t sold—not at first.
ROMAN: But I finally decided that the challenge of starting with a completely clean slate and mapping out a program that would influence astronomy for fifty years was just more than I could turn down.
PADI: That’s how Nancy Grace Roman became NASA’s first chief of astronomy and its first female executive. From the beginning, scientists saw huge opportunities with NASA. You can learn a lot about the universe from telescopes on the ground, but there are limits. Roman says looking through Earth’s atmosphere is something like looking through a stained glass window.
ROMAN: The window has dust on it, so the background is kind of scattered and bright. Next, the glass is colored so that you only see certain colors through it. You only see certain colors through the atmosphere. And we were anxious to see some of the other colors from the universe. And finally, the atmosphere—the glass has defects in it, and that sort of keeps you from getting a sharp picture.
NARRATOR OF “SEAS OF INFINITY”: Yes, it is beyond the air that we must go if we seek a clearer image of the heavens.
JACOB: In the 1960s and ‘70s, NASA made its first attempts to put a telescope in space. It launched a series of four telescopes in a program called OAO: Orbiting Astronomical Observatory.
NARRATOR OF “SEAS OF INFINITY”: When it has been placed in an orbit 500 miles beyond the Earth, this space observatory will give us eyes to see into regions until now invisible to man.
JACOB: The very first OAO satellite, launched in 1966, actually failed once it reached space. But two of the four satellites were successful. They took valuable measurements, especially in ultraviolet light, which Earth’s atmosphere mostly blocks from telescopes on the ground.
PADI: NASA learned a lot from these early space telescopes, and astronomers began to dream even bigger. They wanted to put a more powerful telescope in space. This would eventually become the Hubble Space Telescope, and Nancy Grace Roman was right there from the beginning.
[Music: Goals and Objectives by Eric Chevalier]
ROMAN: My role in Hubble was as program scientist, and that means that I basically tried to sell the program. Did other things too, but my major effort was trying to convince people that it was very well worth doing
PADI: This all started in the sixties, when a group of scientists suggested building a big space telescope.
JACOB: Actually, at the beginning the name of the project was just “Large Space Telescope”. And the details took some ironing out. Some NASA officials saw this as an opportunity for astronauts. They imagined astronauts riding along with the telescope, looking into it and reporting back to Earth.
PADI: Scientists did not like this idea. For one, the astronaut would need to breathe air. The whole point was to put the telescope where there was no air.
ROMAN: Secondly, the man would wiggle. And I don't care how much he tried to stay still, no man or woman is going to sit for an hour without moving. And once he moves in a satellite, the telescope is going to move in the opposite direction. So I definitely knew that the astronomers did not want the man to ride around with it.
PADI: Over the years, the telescope took shape. There were constantly questions to answer and hurdles to get past.
JACOB: How big would the telescope be? Where would the money come from? Who would handle the data and share them with scientists? Behind the scenes, Nancy Grace Roman was a steady hand, keeping the mission moving forward.
ROMAN: So what I did was to bring together a collection of astronomers from all over the country and some NASA engineers and get them to sit down together and come up with something that the engineers thought would work and that the astronomers thought would do their job.
JACOB: Nancy Grace Roman retired as NASA’s chief of astronomy in 1979. At the time, she was taking care of her mother, and she needed to spend more time at home.
PADI: By that point, Hubble was well on its way to the launch pad. And in 1990 ...
[Music: Scientific Progress by Thomas Gallicani]
LAUNCH ANNOUNCER: ... And liftoff of the space shuttle Discovery with the Hubble Space Telescope, our window on the universe.
UNIDENTIFIED VOICE: Congratulations on a super mission. And the world is looking forward to reaping the benefits of your good work over the next 15 years.
JACOB: That was actually 36 years ago.
PADI: Since then, Hubble has changed our fundamental understanding of the universe. Its data have been cited in tens of thousands of research papers and counting.
JACOB: And even for those of us without Ph.D.s, Hubble images spark our imaginations and make us wonder what’s out there.
CHARLES BOLDEN: My favorite image is the deep field image.
JENNIFER WISEMAN: My imagination goes wild. I wonder what it would be like to visit ...
BOLDEN: Galaxies with billions of stars and billions of planets ...
MICHELLE THALLER: Spiral galaxies or kind of blobby elliptical galaxies. They’re actually beautiful little galaxies in and of themselves ...
BOLDEN: ... because it’s one that tells an incredible story about our universe.
PADI: Inside the space agency, people didn’t forget who made it happen. Another NASA official who led the Hubble program nicknamed Nancy Grace Roman “the mother of Hubble”.
JACOB: Years ago, when a senator was asking tough questions about Hubble’s budget, Roman did some quick math to explain why it was worthwhile.
ROMAN: My answer was that for the cost of a night at the movies, every American taxpayer would have 15 years of exciting discoveries. And I may have been off by a factor of three or four, but even if it ended up being one night at the movies every year, I think Hubble has been worth it.
[Music: A Delicate Machine by Jay Price]
JACOB: Nancy Grace Roman died in 2018. She was 93 years old. She left behind a huge legacy. A few years ago, she was even made into a Lego for a “women of NASA” set.
PADI: That happened during her lifetime, and I actually got to celebrate with her and the entire Hubble team. There are still legendary stories about Roman taking copious notes, asking difficult questions, and even knitting during meetings.
JACOB: Outside the clean room where the Roman Space Telescope was built, there’s a photo of Nancy Grace Roman.
PADI: We see her from behind. She has striking white hair, and she’s wearing a beautiful dark blue dress.
JACOB: She’s looking up at NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope, right into its huge, gold mirrors. I always wonder what she was thinking right then, standing so close to one of the telescopes that would carry on Hubble’s legacy and continue to reveal new details about the universe. I do know how she felt about Hubble. Late in her life, Roman recalled seeing one of Hubble’s many, many images of space.
ROMAN: And this was a picture that was taken for engineering purposes. It was not a science picture at all. And just looking at that—with the various colored stars and the whole field just covered with these little colored dots—just blew my mind. That's about all I can say about it.
JOSH SCHLIEDER: When the name became the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, it really took me back, and I was like, "Oh, I recognize that name.”
PADI: This is Josh Schlieder. He’s a NASA scientist.
JOSH: I got my Ph.D. in 2011, trying to identify new nearby young stars in the local part of the galaxy. But in the process I had actually read papers that Nancy Grace Roman wrote in, like, the 1940s and 1950s because she, too, studied nearby young stars.
JACOB: Today, Josh is on the project science team for the Roman Space Telescope. He’s going to help us understand what Roman can do. But he says scientists today—and really, all of us who are curious about the universe—owe a debt to the woman whose name is on the telescope.
JOSH: Without Dr. Nancy Grace Roman and her time at NASA Headquarters and really pushing for NASA to become an agency that prioritizes and works on putting large telescopes in space to do science, we would not be anywhere near where we are today in terms of our general understanding of the universe at large and our place within it.
PADI: To understand what makes Roman special—the secret sauce that sets it apart from other telescopes—let’s go back to its original name. Before it was Roman, it was called the Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope. Roman’s view of the universe is not only deep. It’s wide. Roman will see large parts of the sky, all at once.
JOSH: So if there's anything that I want you and the listeners out there to take away from this conversation about the Roman Space Telescope, it is that Roman is a survey telescope. It's designed to do large scale surveys.
PADI: Roman will lift off from Earth’s surface and travel about a million miles into space. From there, it will spend much of its time methodically scanning parts of the sky.
JACOB: You might have done something similar, if you’ve ever tried to take a panoramic photo. If something is in front of you that’s too big to fit in your camera frame, you can take a photo of a small piece of it. Then move your camera and take another photo, and keep repeating until you have a series of images that you can combine into one complete picture.
PADI: That’s what Roman will be doing in space. What makes Roman so powerful is that its field of view is at least 100 times larger than Hubble’s, and it can also move between observations more quickly than Hubble can.
JOSH: It means that Roman can perform surveys and tile over the sky at a rate—it's about a thousand times faster than Hubble could do it. So we're not talking about Roman doing science that is, you know, just bigger field of view, more sky in one shot than Hubble can do. It's really designed to do science that Hubble can't do.
[Music: Machines Made This by Brian Colin Burrows]
JACOB: Now, Hubble is not going anywhere. Roman is designed to work together with NASA’s other telescopes. Roman has two instruments on board, and it will constantly send us images and an absurd amount of data. Josh is the deputy senior project scientist for Roman’s Wide Field Instrument. With that wide field of view, Roman will give us new information about our own Milky Way Galaxy.
JOSH: And so Roman’s Wide Field Instrument will perform a survey looking toward the center of our galaxy, where there's a very, very large density of stars ...
JACOB: Roman will look for planets in an area with about 200 million stars. And it won’t just look once. It will measure those stars every 12 minutes to look for changes over time that otherwise we wouldn’t see.
JOSH: ... to construct a plot of brightness versus time, and then you can look ...
PADI: Roman will also look beyond our own Milky Way galaxy, to everything else out there.
JOSH: ... where we're observing large numbers of galaxies to measure their properties ...
PADI: ... which is expected to shed light on one of the biggest mysteries in all of physics. More on that in a second.
JACOB: Roman will also survey nearby galaxies and replicate one of Hubble’s most famous images by just staring into the cosmos for a long time.
JOSH: And, you know, other flavors of astrophysics that are really well suited to Roman's wide field survey capability.
PADI: In all, Roman is expected to observe more than a billion galaxies. It will catalog thousands of planets beyond our solar system.
JACOB: There’s a really crazy analogy to put into perspective just how much detail Roman will see. Imagine a 4K TV. A really big one—like, the biggest one you’ve ever seen. No matter what you’re imagining, it’s still not big enough. To fully display Roman’s largest survey, you would need a 4K TV as big as 45 city blocks or big enough to cover El Capitán in Yosemite National Park.
JOSH: What we get out of that is every single image is like a sky panorama with all kinds of interesting things to take a look at.
PADI: So you can see why scientists are excited. All of that data will help us puzzle out some of our biggest questions about the universe.
JACOB: In another episode of this series, we explain more about what it means for exoplanet research, the study of planets outside our solar system, that orbit faraway stars.
PADI: One major mystery that Roman is designed to answer involves the structure of the universe. When scientists map the cosmos, they see that galaxies are not randomly distributed across the sky. There are huge sheets of matter connected by thin strands called filaments.
JOSH: To paint a picture, if you could step way, way back and just look at the universe and see the distribution of galaxies, it kind of looks like a cobweb that you would see up in the corner of your attic or your basement, and we call it literally the cosmic web.
JACOB: The driving forces behind that structure are called dark matter and dark energy.
[Music: Pressurization Trailer by JC Lemay]
If you don’t understand what those are, don’t worry. You’re not alone. To make sense of this dark universe, I called a NASA scientist named Alina Kiessling.
[to Alina] Dark energy is just so strange for most of us that I want to start really at like square zero, if that's OK.
ALINA KIESSLING: Absolutely.
JACOB: What is dark energy? Or what isn't dark energy? Like, I'm not even sure what the right first question is to ask.
ALINA: So dark energy is the name that we give to our ignorance of what is causing the universe to accelerate in its expansion.
JACOB: Scientists have known for about a hundred years that the universe is expanding. That’s not something that affects your daily life, but if you want to know how the universe began—and how it will ultimately end in billions of years—it’s something you need to know. So, we can see regular matter, which is what makes up stars and planets and you and me.
PADI: We can also detect dark matter. Even though it doesn’t interact with normal matter, it has gravity. We can see those effects.
JACOB: For a long time, scientists assumed that the gravity from all the normal matter and dark matter would make the expansion of the universe slow down.
PADI: In the 1990s, they learned that is not the case. The universe is not only expanding—the expansion is getting faster. We have basically no idea what’s making that happen, but we had to put some kind of label on it. And that’s dark energy.
ALINA: There's an analogy that you can kind of think of. If you imagine yourself holding a ball and you throw the ball up in the air and you know that it's going to come back and land in your hand—so this is originally what people thought was happening with the universe, that it would expand out and it would come back down again. But what we found was that the universe was expanding faster and faster, and so that's like if you throw a ball up in the air and then it shoots away from you faster and faster and faster. It's very counterintuitive. People weren't expecting this result.
JACOB: This was so ground-breaking that it led to a Nobel Prize in Physics for two teams of scientists who figured it out at the same time. The Hubble Space Telescope was also a key player, although they don’t give medals to telescopes. Hubble observations of a particular type of exploding star helped astronomers measure the distances to faraway galaxies, and with those measurements they could figure out how much the universe was expanding. Before Hubble, dark energy was something nobody expected. Now it’s a huge priority for people like Alina.
ALINA: We just know so little about it. We understand what it's doing. We understand that it's causing the universe to accelerate in its expansion, to get faster and faster as it's expanding, but we really know nothing else. So, while you asked me to start at ground zero and give you the five-minute introduction, I think you and your listeners now know as much about dark energy as most of the scientists.
PADI: Roman will shed some light on dark energy in a few ways.
[Music: Tentative Surge by Jan Telegra]
It will measure the same types of exploding stars that led to the discovery of dark energy in the first place—but boatloads more. It will take advantage of wrinkles in the fabric of space-time, which magnify galaxies that are really far away. And it will detect the imprint of primordial sound waves that have lingered almost from the birth of the universe itself.
With all of that information, Roman will make detailed, 3D maps of the universe. One of the big questions about dark energy is, has it changed and is it still changing over time? Roman will help us get closer to that answer. There are already signs that dark energy might clash with our existing standard model of the universe. Physicists might have to go back to the drawing board and figure out a new model—a new way of describing really basic properties of the universe. This is the kind of thing that astronomers get jazzed about.
ALINA: I think universally all the scientists that I work with are very excited by the prospect of there being something that we don't yet understand. So I'm not saying that we'll definitely find this. There's still a chance that we would find that dark energy is constant, that the standard model of cosmology is actually correct. But if we do find something that is not the standard model, that's super exciting, potentially Nobel Prize-winning science.
JACOB: At this point, I should tell you a little more about Alina Kiessling. She works at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, and she is a particular type of astronomer called a cosmologist. Those are the folks who look at the structure of the universe and how it began and how it will ultimately end.
For a project as big as Roman, it really takes a village. Alina is part of a whole community of scientists who have been preparing for years. She started working on Roman in 2012. Once Roman launches, all those scientists will have years’ more work ahead of them. The survey data will reveal objects that are so far away or so hard to detect that scientists can just barely make them out.
ALINA: We have to measure these very, very tiny galaxies. These are a couple of pixels that are kind of fuzzy at best on the sky, and we're trying to measure the shape of these galaxies exceptionally precisely.
JACOB: Think back to that gigantic 4K screen—the one as big as the side of a mountain. Scientists will comb through every pixel, squeezing out as much information as they can.
ALINA: And so it takes a really long time for the scientists to—what's the word—perfect the techniques to do these analyses.
[Music: Gene Sequencing by Al Lethbridge]
PADI: Alina is the principal investigator for a project called OpenUniverse, which is one of the tools to practice these techniques. OpenUniverse uses a supercomputer to simulate the entire universe—or at least what we know so far.
ALINA: Including everything that we know about what galaxies look like, how they're distributed on the sky, and all the time we're updating and improving the models of what the universe looks like, so that those simulations of the galaxy catalogs look as close to reality as possible.
JACOB: Once they have their supercomputer universe, scientists rehearse looking at it. They use the specs and technical details from Roman to understand exactly how their simulated universe would look through the telescope’s eyes.
ALINA: And this is really important part, because the telescopes introduce distortions or changes to the image in ways that we have to understand when we're trying to make these very, very precise measurements. And so we're able to do that, they can—the telescope optics, like the mirrors, can actually change the colors of things that we're seeing, or the shapes, so we really need to understand what's going on there.
PADI: The OpenUniverse team has published some of its simulated images. You can go on NASA’s website and see videos with five years of simulated observations.
JACOB: Another scientist who worked on the project called it “the largest, deepest, most realistic synthetic survey of a mock universe available today.”
PADI: But no matter how good the simulation is, it will soon be overshadowed by the real thing. After years of preparation, Roman will show us surprises in the real universe that the simulation could never predict.
ALINA: It's very surreal. So, how does it feel to work on something that almost feels theoretical? Because I'm not physically touching any of the hardware, I'm just thinking about the science. And it's very strange to think of this shift that we're going to have from “Theoretically what is Roman going to see?” to “This is what Roman sees.”
JACOB: Whenever I hear people talk about their work on these NASA projects that take years or decades of their career, I always think, “I don't know if I could do that.” Like, I don't know if I'm built for that. Do you ever have moments when it's just hard to keep that focus or you even get discouraged or frustrated or anything like that?
ALINA: This is such a dynamically changing field that it's really easy to stay engaged for long periods of time, and also you get to know the people that you're working with across the world really well, and so you're working with a huge cohort of people that become your really great friends, and you have really lively debates about what to do next. There are times when you have a particularly challenging problem that takes you weeks, months to solve, and it can become a little discouraging, but it's also the payoff when you resolve that problem. You just feel so elated that it's why you keep going.
[Music: Ancient Starlight by Al Lethbridge]
JACOB: Alina is one half of a NASA power couple. So when she talks about making bonds with other astronomers, she really means it. Her husband Jason is also a cosmologist. He also works at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he also works on Roman. In fact, if you want a Curious Universe deep cut, you can hear him talking about dark matter and dark energy in an episode from a few years ago.
As Roman was about to be packed up and sent to the launch site, there was a friends and family day where people who worked on the mission could give it one last look. Alina and Jason have one-year-old twins. Alina stayed home with them, and Jason went to say goodbye to Roman.
ALINA: My husband was able to take our five-year-old. They've got such lovely photos of the two of them in front of the telescope. I mean, you can't be in the clean room. It was in the viewing gallery, which the five-year-old was deeply incensed about. She thought she was going to be allowed to go up and touch it.
JACOB: [laughs]
ALINA: Yeah.
JACOB: Alina and Jason first met working together on another space telescope. That one is called Euclid. Euclid was built by the European Space Agency with NASA contributions, and it launched in 2023. Alina has actually been working for that one even longer. She started in 2006. We don’t have time to fully go into Euclid here, but it is also a powerful telescope that will work closely with Roman to investigate dark energy and other big mysteries. Anyway, seeing Euclid leave this planet was a powerful experience.
[Music: Beyond Our Imagination by Timothy James Cornick and Matthew Jacob Loveridge]
ALINA: It was probably one of the more emotional things that I've ever experienced in my life. It's visceral. It's very physical. You're miles away. You can't get super close, but the sound is physical. It just washed through your whole body. It was very, very loud, and you could feel your whole body vibrating. And watching it go up, honestly I had tears in my eyes. This telescope, Euclid, that I'd been working on for about 20 years had had gone up into space and successfully launched, and it was a beautiful moment. So everybody should try to watch a rocket launch one day.
JACOB: For Roman, Alina expects to feel that all over again. She and Jason are both traveling to the launch, and they will not be alone.
ALINA: We're planning on taking the whole family down. My five-year-old's old enough now to understand what's going on, and so we'll be able to bring our five-year-old along and really share that experience, and we can tell the one-year-olds about it later. (laughs)
PADI: Now, at the time this episode comes out, launch of the Roman Space Telescope is so close. It’s coming, but it’s not here yet. And for the people working on this telescope, including Josh Schlieder, it’s not time to celebrate just yet.
JACOB: What does it feel like to be kind of in this moment right now?
JOSH: I mean, if I'm brutally honest: tired. It feels tiring. But it's also like there's a lot of anticipation.
JACOB: Even in the home stretch before launch, the Roman team is not sitting still. When I talked to Josh, he was fresh off a test that rehearsed the process of bringing Roman online once it’s in space.
PADI: Roman will be the latest tool in NASA’s toolbox, but it won’t work alone. Roman will tag-team with other observatories, including Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescope. We’ll uncover a clearer picture of the universe from this fleet of telescopes, including the survey data coming from Roman.
JOSH: We can feed that back into Hubble. We can go observe it in the ultraviolet, where Roman has no sensitivity. We can feed it into the James Webb Space Telescope, which goes deeper into the infrared, beyond Roman's wavelength range, and has a larger aperture to get much more sensitive measurements. And both Hubble and Webb, and many other telescopes on the ground and in space—they have these complementary capabilities that I think Roman will really be a discovery machine, and finding interesting things out there in the universe, and then those interesting things will filter down and become targets for individual study with all these other observatories.
JACOB: On another level, Roman’s images will be beautiful.
[Music: Points of Light by Jay Woods]
Hubble and Webb have the power to spark our imaginations, even if most of us don’t understand all the science contained in those images. What will it mean when we see images that are 100 times wider than Hubble? Even though we have simulations, we won’t know until we see the real thing.
JOSH: Every single image is going to be a sea of stars and galaxies. And we kind of have a sense of what that will look like, but I think seeing the real thing will just touch a different nerve. It'll be the real deal. It'll be a real image of something out there in the universe, a real sky scene, and you know it'll be the first time we've ever seen it in this way.
PADI: Roman will try to answer science questions from the telescopes that came before it, but it will surely find new questions to ask. Somewhere in those thousands of exoplanets and billions of galaxies are details scientists could never predict.
JOSH: If you just think about the numbers, if you have 2 billion galaxies that you've detected, and you can say, "OK, I've measured the brightness and these bands for these 2 billion galaxies,” that means that within that part of the sky, there's 2,000 things that are one in a million in that survey.
JACOB: That’s pretty cool.
JOSH: That's how I like to think about the power of this observatory. That's the kind of thing that I think is really cool, that I think is really going to give people new opportunities to think about our universe and really learn something new, is the unexpected.
JACOB: This is NASA’s Curious Universe, an official NASA podcast. This episode was written and produced by me, Jacob Pinter. Our team also includes Christian Elliott. Our executive producer is Katie Konans.
Wes Buchanan and Krystofer Kim designed the show art for this series. Our theme song is by SYSTEM Sounds. Special thanks to Claire Andreoli, Calla Cofield, Alise Fisher, and Colin McNutt.
Some of the clips of Nancy Grace Roman came from an oral history that belongs to the NASA History Office. Special thanks to Sandra Johnson for providing the audio. The NASA History Office is an incredible resource, and you can find much more, including more oral histories, at nasa.gov/history.
We also had research help from the Niels Bohr Library and Archives at the American Institute of Physics and the Annual Review of Astronomy and Astrophysics.
You can find transcripts for every episode of Curious Universe and explore NASA’s other podcasts at nasa.gov/podcasts.
If you enjoyed this episode of NASA’s Curious Universe … let us know! Leave us a review wherever you’re listening right now. Why not send a link to one of your friends. And you can follow NASA’s Curious Universe in your favorite podcast app to get a notification each time we post a new episode.

item.content:encoded: Far away from us, around distant stars, scientists have already found thousands of these exoplanets. Roman will look toward the center of our own Milky Way. Where it can see literally hundreds of thousands of stars in a single image at once. We know that most stars have planets. Which means Roman will detect thousands more exoplanets out there. With a cutting-edge piece of technology, Roman will see far more detail of some planets than we've ever seen before. These planets are so incredibly faint that you get one photon, one particle of light. Arriving at our camera from one of those planets once every few seconds or maybe even once every minute. So we are getting one little smudge to try to tease out what the atmosphere might be made of.

item.content:encoded:
[Music: Castles in Space by Richard John Hampson]
HUBBLE LAUNCH ANNOUNCER: T-minus 10. Go for main engine start.
HOST PADI BOYD: NASA is about to send a powerful new telescope into space—the latest in a legacy of exploration.
HOST JACOB PINTER: First there was Hubble.
HUBBLE LAUNCH ANNOUNCER: And liftoff of the space shuttle Discovery with the Hubble Space Telescope, our window on the universe.
JACOB: Then the James Webb Space Telescope, designed to show us cosmic dawn.
ROB NAVIAS, NASA COMMUNICATIONS: From a tropical rain forest to the edge of time itself, James Webb begins a voyage back to the birth of the universe.
PADI: Every new telescope—every new tool—reveals something unexpected.
JULIE MCENERY: That was crazy.
JOSH SCHLIEDER: If you have 2 billion galaxies, there’s 2,000 things that are one in a million.
ALINA KIESSLING: It’s very counterintuitive. People weren’t expecting this result.
PADI: Now, a new NASA telescope is ready to join them in exploring the biggest mysteries out there.
[several experts say “Roman”]
JULIE: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
[Music: Cloud Network by Christopher John White]
JACOB: Get ready for NASA’s new view of the universe and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope with a special limited series of NASA’s Curious Universe.
PADI: Roman has a wide field of view that will capture a huge swath of the sky.
JOSH: Every single image is going to be a sea of stars and galaxies.
JACOB: … and provide scientists with incredible new details about space.
JULIE: So we’re going to study the things that we know about, and we’re going to find the things we didn’t even know to look for.
JACOB: On Curious Universe, we dive into the science behind the Roman Space Telescope.
PADI: No Ph.D. required.
JULIE: So you’re asking for the 10-second description of how the universe entirely works. (laughs)
[Music: Pressurization Trailer by JC Lemay]
JACOB: Roman will investigate a mysterious force called dark energy. So far, experts have more questions about dark energy than answers.
ALINA: We just know so little about it. So, while you asked me to start at ground zero and give you the five-minute introduction, I think you and your listeners now know as much about dark energy as most of the scientists.
PADI: But Roman is designed to shed light on dark energy, and what we find could make astronomers rethink some basic information we thought we knew about the universe.
ALINA: That’s super exciting, potentially Nobel Prize-winning science.
PADI: Roman will also discover and study planets beyond our solar system.
[Music: Case Notes by Terell Omar Farrell]
JACOB: Far away from us around distant stars, scientists have already found thousands of these exoplanets. Roman will look toward the center of our own Milky Way.
VANESSA BAILEY: … where it can see literally hundreds of thousands of stars in a single image at once. We know that most stars have planets.
JACOB: … which means Roman will detect thousands more exoplanets out there.
PADI: With a cutting-edge piece of technology, Roman will see far more detail of some planets than we’ve ever seen before.
VANESSA: These planets are so incredibly faint that you get one photon—one particle of light—arriving at our camera from one of those planets once every few seconds or maybe even once every minute. So we are getting one little smudge to try to tease out what the atmosphere might be made of.
PADI: In our series, we’ll also meet the engineers who make NASA space telescopes.
[Music: Dots and Dashes by Jan Telegra]
MARK MELTON: We’re building one-of-a-kind satellites. It’s never been built before. No one’s going to build this again.
JACOB: You’ll get up close with technicians as they carefully assemble Roman inside a huge clean room.
PADI: And visit a specialized test chamber that mimics the extreme environment of space—mostly.
MATT STEPHENS: I mean, we’re artificially making space in there, right? We’re making a vacuum. We’re making the temperatures. We’re doing everything we can but turn off gravity, because we can’t do that, right?
JACOB: Along the way, NASA experts will help us understand what it all means for scientists and engineers and also for the rest of us, just trying to wrap our minds around what’s out there.
ALINA: It’s very surreal.
MARK: And I sat down, and I got a little tear in my eye, and I kind of choked up, like, wow … (fade out)
JOSH: It’ll be a real image of something out there in the universe, a real sky scene, and, you know, it’ll be the first time we’ve ever seen it in this way.
JULIE: The most exciting science is going to be the thing that you didn’t expect.
MARK: … which is kind of crazy to me.
PADI: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launches soon.
JACOB: And so does a special limited series all about Roman right here on NASA’s Curious Universe, an official NASA podcast.
PADI: New episodes coming soon.
JULIE: And then the fun really begins.

item.title: The USS Monitor, Part 1: History and Legacy
item.description: 【节目】NOAA Ocean Podcast 【主题】ocean-environment 【形态】audio, text 【生产形态】full-episode, text-script 【摘要】USS Monitor 的前传：1862 年内战铁甲舰为何而建、百日赶工、旋转炮塔如何改写海战，又为何沉没后反而成了第一个国家海洋保护区和人工礁。 【Reels 角度】铁甲舰的前传：Monitor 用 100 天赶造出来、炮塔一转就改写海战，沉了之后反而成了受保护的礁。 【许可证】Public domain：美国联邦政府作品（NOAA 官方播客），一般不受版权保护 【权利说明】可剪辑/再分发，不得暗示 NOAA 背书；本集文字稿中未见第三方歌曲标注；片段为原声对话，无 BGM。 【来源】https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/podcast/july26/nop84-uss-history-legacy.html 【采集日（北京时间）】2026-11-02 【发布时间精度】date_only（NOAA 官方单集页 DC.date.created meta：2026-7-20（仅到日，RSS 时间以当日 00:00 UTC 占位，精度字段已注明，不伪造具体时刻）） 【子片段 GUID】urn:podcast:oceanservice.noaa.gov:podcast:july26:nop84-uss-history-legacy:clip:turret:132.2-180.3
item.content:encoded: HOST: This is the NOAA Ocean Podcast. I’m your host, Allison Burrell. Throughout our coasts and Great Lakes lie myriad shipwrecks, some still yet to be found. The focus today is the USS Monitor, where its resting place serves as the first U.S. National Marine Sanctuary. Let’s go back in time to the U.S. Civil War in 1862. The USS Monitor, a first of its kind Civil War ironclad, sinks 16 miles off the coast of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. We are joined in the studio by Maritime Archeologist, Tane Casserley, from the Office of National Marine Sanctuaries, whose specialties include 19th-century warships and deep-water archaeology. In the first of two episodes we discuss the history of the USS Monitor, its legacy, and why it is still important today. Now let’s dive in… I'd like to welcome our guest, Tane Casserley. Thanks for joining us at the NOAA Ocean podcast. TANE CASSERLEY: Excited to be here. Thank you for having me. HOST: First of all, why do we study shipwrecks? TANE CASSERLEY: It's a good question, why do we study shipwrecks. And I look at shipwrecks, is that they're a window to our past. Now, it could be a window looking through, at the technology, because a lot of times when you look at ships back to the age of antiquity, those were almost sort of the phase ships of their time, right? The technological marvels, what they're able to do. But they're also windows back into people's lives and their cultures. So it's always any angle you want to take with it you can learn something from these shipwrecks as we study them. HOST: We're talking about this amazing ship, the Monitor. Why is this shipwreck significant? What's the history behind this, I'm guessing, well preserved shipwreck? TANE CASSERLEY: Well, first, it's a technological marvel. Monitor was a prototype. It was the first of its kind ever and it's basically the ancestor of every modern naval vessel today. And it goes back to, you know, If you think about the way ships might be in the age of sail, right? You get the tall ships and all of these guns. But when the ship goes down and is spotting another vessel, the entire ship has to turn because the guns are pointing out from the sides of it. So you go forward, you turn, you fire. So, that was done for hundreds of years. But what made Monitor unique was it now separated the move into the gun from the movement of the vessel. So the vessel could be in any orientation. And because Monitor had the world's first revolving gun turret that went into battle, it was able to move in any direction as well. So that was a huge marker in the change of these technologies. And also, we can't forget that it's a transition from that wooden warship, those wooden walls, now iron and metal, which is modern naval warfare. HOST: So the design of the Monitor is very unique for its time and this was during the Civil War in the late 1800s, right? TANE CASSERLEY: In 1861 is when it was being built and it was launched in 1862. HOST: So why was this particular iron clad ship built? Because there's a great story behind that. TANE CASSERLEY: The concept of an iron warship wasn't new at the time. People were experimenting with this and they knew that, iron, much like armor on a knight. In the sort of medieval days, it protected the person inside. So these iron warships did the same thing. So we’re really getting into the industrial age and like, you know, late 1700s, early 1800s. We're able to manufacture these things. We can create iron plate, right? We developed riveting. So now these big metal plates can be held together. It was a concept that was known, but not a lot of people had adopted it because also it's very expensive to do this. In the early 1860s, 1861, the South was moving back up into Virginia to these northern, Union held lands. Right, So they came into an area known as Portsmouth, Virginia, which is here in Hampton Roads, Virginia. They took over the Gosport Navy Yard. The Union knew this was happening and they didn't want the South to get any of their equipment, supplies, or ships, right? So what they couldn't take with them, they destroyed. They left cannons; they destroyed them. They left gunpowder; they blew it up. They had naval stores, like food and rations; burned them. And, they just so happened to have a vessel that was being repaired, the USS Merrimack, an older steam frigate at dock. It was under repairs that weren't able to move it so they decided to burn that ship at the dock and sink it. So belief is, don't let the South get it. But, the South knew that this ship was there and they already had plans and how to adapt if they could get themselves ahold of a Union vessel or something in that size, how they could adapt that ship into an iron clad because they didn't have that industrial base to really build these things like the North did. So they had to adapt and overcome. So that's what they did. So they see that vessel there. They raise it, they put it into dry dock, and essentially from the water line up, they totally rebuild it into this Confederate monster. 200 plus feet long, iron plated, just unstoppable force. HOST: And that's the USS Virginia? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, well, so that's so when the South was rebuilding it. That's when we think that rebuilding time we start calling it the CSS Virginia because it is fundamentally changed, at that point. HOST: Oh, CSS, the Confederate. TANE CASSERLEY: The CSS the Confederate state ships. The South were building this because it was unstoppable. The unit had nothing that could go against it, so they knew that, like on a naval front with tactics, they had a weapon. But they also used propaganda. There were drawings of things of this ship being built. It wasn't a secret news being built. The North knew it. They hurriedly put together, under Abraham Lincoln's guidance, the iron clad board, to take in designs to something that could counter that Confederate threat. What can counter that CSS Virginia that's being built? And the design that eventually made it through was the Monitor. This crazy unique thing that's never been seen before. Monitor was a prototype, you can't forget. Nothing like it's been built like it before. That's what they put forward to battle the Virginia. HOST: They're building the Monitor in response to the South building this half submersible? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, and imagine these poor guys right who are used to working on open decks, working the masts and the sails in the open air. Now they're told you're going to work in this, what looks like to be an iron coffin. You can't see the sky, it's hot, and you just hope to all the heaven above that you don't sink, because this thing is so strange looking. But they did, they all volunteered to do it. HOST: I bet there wasn't very good airflow down there. TANE CASSERLEY: It had some force ventilators and things, but it took a little adapting things to make sure we had some good airflow, so it was a little stuffy and it could be very hot at times. HOST: The history behind the Monitor is so interesting and I'm just curious because this was during the Civil War period, were there any notable historical figures associated with this ship that we might be familiar with? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, well, the most exciting one was President Abraham Lincoln. So he visited the ship twice, so he actually walked the decks. He was honored, he went inside, he went into the engine room, and it's really because this ship was so incredible and was so different, it instantly became an icon. Of course, after the Battle of Hampton Roads, what the Union says, you know, the Monitor won the battle. Abraham Lincoln has to go down there to see that ship and to praise the crew. You know, it's incredible. It's just amazing to me that he was on that vessel that we get to work with every day. HOST: And there's almost photographic evidence of this. TANE CASSERLEY: There is. In July of 1862, a photographer came to Monitor, and it was supposed to be to document Lincoln coming again to visit the ship. And unfortunately, the two missed each other, so there's these fantastic historic photographs of the crew and the officers on the deck of Monitor. So we have that, right? So, you know, we get that glimpse back in time. But unfortunately, we did miss Abraham Lincoln being on it. But he was there too. HOST: I bet that photographer was kicking himself for missing the opportunity to photograph a president. TANE CASSERLEY: He's a very famous guy called Gibson, so I'm thinking he maybe had other opportunities. HOST: But I guess this was before there was a staff photographer that just followed the president around? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, well, again, you think about the 1860s where the practice of photography was also a newer practice as well. Yeah, that's why we would love to, if we have more images of Monitor, but we have what we have and we're grateful for it. HOST: So the Monitor is in saltwater, but what's the difference between salt and freshwater shipwrecks? TANE CASSERLEY: Shipwrecks in freshwater generally are very well preserved. So that cold, fresh, water, you can almost think of it like a chiller or freezer, you know, type of thing where you don't have those salts that are going to intrude into the metals and into the other sort of materials on a shipwreck. So it keeps it very well preserved. So oftentimes in the Great Lakes, especially very deep, the preservation's near perfect, like it's amazing, you know, what you can see down there. You could open up a trunk and you could see clothing, fabrics, hats. You know, that's so well preserved in that cold freshwater. It's stunning. We have national marine sanctuaries in the Great Lakes that are fantastic to visit to see that. The challenge in saltwater is that the marine life and especially those salts basically attack those materials. It may be that you have wood boring mollusks that are going to eat the wood remains of a shipwreck. So they eat all the wood and you're just left with the metal fittings. It could be, you know, you've got other marine life that are moving things around or digging through things. And the biggest challenge of course is going to be that salt. And Monitor’s an iron ship in saltwater. And if you know anything about iron and salt, they don't mix. It was deteriorating at an accelerated rate when we really started studying Monitor in the 80s and 90s. So we had to make a decision about what we're going to do with that vessel. HOST: How and when was the Monitor found? TANE CASSERLEY: In the late 60s, early 70s, there were several expeditions going out to try to find the Monitor, where it sank up the coast of North Carolina off Cape Hatteras. So, we have the ship logs. You know, we can look historically at what the storms and currents were doing at the time, the way the winds were. So, it was a group out of Beauford, North Carolina out of Duke University. Going out there with MIT, National Geographic, the North Carolina, their sort of history and archives division with their maritime archaeologist. And they went out in ‘73 searching for the Monitor using the USS Rhode Island's logbook and looking at a whole bunch of other factors. And the USS Rhode Island was the vessel that was towing the Monitor when it sank, so they had a lot of really great information. As it happens, almost in every expedition, on the very last day of their survey going out, they find what they call a long amorphous echo on their side scan sonar on the sea floor. And what they expected to see with this sonar in the sonar is really think of it like it's creating an image through sound. So you use that to look at the sea floor or other things. They expected to find a vessel with two pointy ends and a round protuberance in the center. And that is not what they found, right? They found what appeared to be a shipwreck on the bottom that was long, it had a pointy end, and sort of a crushed broken stern and that was it. So like, whoa, it seems to be the Monitor, but it's not quite this isn't what we expect to see. And they did put down a drop camera and a drop video camera. But you kind of remember back in the 70s, these were hazy black and white images. They're seeing maybe four or five square feet down there, you know, they can't really control it. So it literally took them a year of going through all those images and things to really stare at it. And it was actually one of my mentors, my graduate school in East Carolina University, Dr. Gordon Watts, who was that maritime archaeologist from North Carolina on the ship. He posed the question, what happens if the ship is upside down? And then all the pieces came together. The turret is underneath, the ship's upside down and they go back out in ‘74. They get a better image of it in ‘75, they're like, this is it. HOST: This is it. Wow, that's so interesting. Yeah, you're just not thinking, oh, what if it flipped over as it sank? How deep is the Monitor? TANE CASSERLEY: 240 feet. They do the currents really move the sediments around, so it does vary a little bit. But if we were diving we would call it a 240 table. HOST: So can scuba divers investigate this ship? Is 240 feet doable? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah. Absolutely. But yeah, it's a technical dive. So, you know, you've got to be properly trained, you have the right equipment. But the shipwreck, the purpose of it as well is to to open it up so recreational divers can visit it. HOST: How far off shore is the Monitor? TANE CASSERLEY: The Monitor is about 16 and a half miles off the coast of Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. HOST: OK, so it's pretty far. It's pretty far out there. TANE CASSERLEY: It's, I mean, you could, you know, it's an hour or two out of the harbor. But what makes it so challenging out there is that, you know, Cape Hatteras is known for the storms. It's known for the rough weather. And that happens all the time. So even with our dive expeditions, we would expect to lose at least half the days because of those challenges of just the marine operations offshore. You never know what you're going to get out there. HOST: Now, I'm going to compare it to a very well known shipwreck, the Titanic. You were saying mollusks and the salt are all degrading it. Now, this ship is even older than the Titanic. Is it disintegrating at the same speed as the Titanic? Or is it in better condition or worse condition? I'm just curious. TANE CASSERLEY: Well, it's a good question. The difference between Monitor and the Titanic. Both, you know, metal hulled vessels in that marine environment. But you know, there's such different environments. To be honest, you know, the pH is different. The temperature’s different. So I think in some ways, it's very difficult to compare the two because they are so different. I mean, even the base hull materials are different. So I couldn't say which one is better preserved, because there's so many other factors that come into play. But, I will say with all ship wrecks over time, they will come to a point where they will collapse. So some of those iconic views that we have of it, it's just how nature works with these structures. You know, they will collapse over time. But that doesn't change how special they are. They're still grave sites. That doesn't change at all. It's just the way you look at it might be a little different. HOST: But I mean, they're 50 years apart, approximately. And the Monitor is still there. It hasn't collapsed yet? There's still… TANE CASSERLEY: You know, the Monitor is still in great shape. Well, we have to remember too that the two vessels were made for very different purposes. So Titanic, you know, open ocean luxury passenger liner. Very specific. So the Monitor is also very specific where it's an iron clad built warship with an iron hull. I think that the Monitor was built so stoutly to withstand these cannonballs and things with its deck. It's that armor belt that wraps around it. It's almost now that the ship is upside down, I believe that's really creating a protective framework to hold the Monitor together. So it's really done us a favor that it protected it during its years in battle and war. But that armor belt is really protecting it now as a thriving reef. HOST: The Union navy was building this ship in response to the South building a ship. How long did it take to build Monitor? TANE CASSERLEY: Well, so since Monitor was being built, the whole reason it was being built is in response to the construction of the CSS Virginia. And because the CSS Virginia was so much further along in that construction process, stipulation with the construction of Monitor was, this ship had to be built in a hundred days. HOST: Wow, a hundred days. That sounds really short. TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, it's incredibly short for this type of ship that's never been seen or built before. Almost what happens today with shipbuilding or naval construction is that the contract goes out to manufacturers in the region. So in the Northeast, scores of manufacturers are requested to build parts of the vessel. The iron plate for it. Here's where the wood’s coming from. Here's where some of the engines are coming from. Here's where the steam machinery is coming from, and that it all comes together at Greenpoint, New York, where it's all built at the shipyard there and comes together. So it's incredible that not only were many of these things designed just for Monitor and unique that had to be built, that they all came together and they actually worked is incredible. HOST: And who is the designer behind this ship? TANE CASSERLEY: So the designer of Monitor is a brilliant man named John Erickson, he's a Swedish engineer. He's an immigrant to the U.S. and just an incredible man in terms of what he designed, developed, came up with. And also a man of a large personality. He was a very proud man, very proud of Monitor. He let people know it. HOST: I bet he helped, that personality helped, with pushing this build through in a hundred days. TANE CASSERLEY: Oh, absolutely, absolutely. It's just a force of will. But also people knew he was a brilliant engineer. The concepts seem completely crazy. They knew it would probably work, but you know, he did have controversy where people thought, you know, Erickson's folly, they called the Monitor. Right? This thing is going to launch and then slip right underneath the water and hit the bottom of the Hudson River. But Erickson, being again a man of strong will and personality, said, I'm going to stand on the deck as this ship is launched. And I'll prove to you the ship will float and it did. HOST: I mean, I bet there are a lot of skeptics out there. All this iron, it's super heavy. How the heck is it going to float? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, it's incredible. And it's so again, we have to think back then in the 1860s, it was such a strange concept to look at. It was so different. I mean, it truly looked like something that you would bury somebody in. So he proved them wrong. HOST: So did they start building more iron clad ships? TANE CASSERLEY: They did. Well, and funny thing was. So the Monitor was built in response to the Virginia. This was not initially supposed to be the next wave of U.S. Navy warships or design. But in some ways, it did become that. So they built over 60 of these Monitor-style vessels. HOST: 60? TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, over 60. It's incredible because it just became so iconic with the U.S. Navy. And there was so much momentum of this American design vessel that it really became an iconic part of the U.S. naval history and what we became known for in the mid-late 1800s. HOST: Were they all built out of that Brooklyn shipyard? TANE CASSERLEY: No, once they had the initial designs, John Erickson did have a few different types of Monitors. But then other naval engineers came in as well. And they put their own touches. You know, it could be that Monitor had one turret. Well, now some Monitors had some Monitor-style warships had two turrets, right? Monitor head one propeller. Some had two. Some had different kinds of hulls. So what's exciting is to see that evolution, right? Or how they built on that design. But also when you start looking at the hull, getting a little more of a V shape. You know, the hull coming a little more up out of the water to go into bigger seas. And now what we're starting to see is the precursor to battleships. All leading back to Monitor that started this whole thing. HOST: We can attribute the Monitor to the game battleship that I played as a kid. That’s amazing. TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, no, absolutely. You know, those are very famous sort of American World War II battleships that we've seen in movies time and time again. You know, the working of that turret and its design is very similar to the Monitor. And it's only separated by 70 years, 80 years? HOST: That’s amazing. TANE CASSERLEY: A difference in scale, of course. But it's essentially the same thing, which is amazing. HOST: It's a shame that the Monitor sank. But because it did, it's somewhat preserved. And we can go and look at it and see its design and see some of the unique design features. Some of the future iterations of Monitor, like the Passaic, that ended up being sold for scrap metal. So if the Monitor hadn't sank, maybe eventually it would have been decommissioned, sold to someone, and turned into scrap. And we would have no historical record of the actual first ironclad ship that is responsible for the design of all our future battleships. TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, well, I think that's one of the most amazing things about shipwrecks. If you think about some of these naval ships with their lifespan, sometimes they do survive the entire war, and they have long lives, and then they're sold off and do different things, or they're scrapped. But some of them, but they're lost. They're gone to history, but some of them, when they go down in a shipwreck, that is the classic preserved time capsule. Everything is from that battle, from that storm, what those men on board, the sailors, the officers, the crew, what they were going through, and those final moments, you know, are still there. So those stories that we told of that are timeless and priceless. HOST: Well, and what's so interesting is it's not just a historical record that's down there. There is wildlife that is thriving. So what kind of wildlife lives on and around this wreck, because I'm sure it's different in different parts of the ocean. TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah, and absolutely. We've seen that time and time again. When we do our NOAA expeditions out to the Monitor, or really any shipwreck site, when we work through the National Marine Sanctuary, is that we're looking at the ship historically, archeologically, but also as a marine habitat, right? Those are all very important functions that that ship or that site has. Yeah, it's exciting to go down, and now you see it's gone from that weapon of war to an island of life. And when you look at the environment to the sea floor off North Carolina, it really is a desert environment. In a lot of respects, lots of sand. There is live rock and live bottom and things too, but it's very patchy. So when you get these wrecks, especially these larger wrecks, the marine life does accumulate there. So you see the smaller fish and the juveniles and things that are living on it, bringing in the larger fish, and the larger fish after that, and then the predators. And then, you know, we get this beautiful covering of soft corals and sponges and things. And the whole site has now come alive with these vibrant colors. So it's exciting to see that that's another story we can tell about Monitor. It's not just a warship, it's not just going through the battle, or not just being defined by the sinking. It's now being defined as its role today. What makes it so exciting to talk about Monitor or even to visit it in different ways, is that a, you know, you sort of you choose your adventure. What do you want to explore Monitor? It's up to you. HOST: And if that ship wasn't there, would there be as much of a concentration of wildlife nearby? TANE CASSERLEY: No, no. If the ship wasn't there, it would just be a sandy bottom. So really, it is providing that extra habitat, which is incredible. HOST: That's incredible. TANE CASSERLEY: We can't forget Monitor was cold fired. It didn't use petroleum products, it didn't use oil. So all of those things are pretty inert down there. So there's nothing else that's damaging or toxic for that marine life. Really, it really just provides a really nice strata for everything to live and grow on. HOST: So the Monitor is a National Marine Sanctuary. And you work for the Office of National Marine Sanctuaries here at the National Ocean Service. What is the significance of being designated a marine sanctuary? TANE CASSERLEY: Well, first I should mention, Monitor’s the first sanctuary. HOST: Wow. TANE CASSERLEY: We're very proud of that. Designated back in 1975. HOST: So the first ironclad ship and the first marine sanctuary. TANE CASSERLEY: Absolutely. Yes. So we're very proud that, you know, we're also the smallest. But National Marine Sanctuaries, you know, of course, you're going to be thinking about national parks and things in the same vein. And very similar to that, but you know, national marine sanctuaries, they're there to really highlight, celebrate, protect and manage these incredible resources that belong to the public. So whether it be historical, cultural, indigenous, technological, biological with reefs, you know, fish, invertebrates, whales. Each one of our sanctuaries focuses on a particular aspect or collection aspects of those things to protect and celebrate these things that are so special in our marine environment. You know, whether it's in the ocean, rivers on the Great Lakes. We would love to protect all shipwrecks, but you know, sometimes it's just not able to do that. But in our sanctuaries, many of them are dedicated to just protecting shipwrecks. A lot of them in the Great Lakes, you know, Monitor of course. There's the Mallows Bay Potomac River in the Potomac River. But a lot of our sanctuaries too protect shipwrecks alongside those biological resources. So the marine life, the local ecology, the beautiful whales and things, you know. So it really is, it's an incredible organization to work for with this sort of vast management responsibility, with some of these resources that are dwindling. So it's incredible to be part of that to help preserve it for American people. HOST: So the Monitor is 16 miles offshore. So obviously, if the public comes down, they're not going to get on a ship and go two hours out to the sanctuary. So there is the Mariners’ Museum. And it's the proud home to the USS Monitor Center. You house over 5,000 artifacts and over 200 tons of archaeological material that's been recovered from the Monitor shipwreck. What artifacts were brought up from the wreck and why were they chosen in particular? TANE CASSERLEY: Well, that's a good question. You know, we partnered with the Mariners’ Museum Park here in Newport News, Virginia. We started that relationship back in 1987, because we realized as a sanctuary, we needed a place to put our archival documents. But also when we started recovering smaller items from the shipwreck, where can that go to be conserved properly, but also the most importantly displayed for the public. You know, when we look at artifacts, you’ve got to think about a couple things. First of all, the act of recovering it from the sea floor and bringing it to the surface is not the end of the project. That's like the first fifth of what you have to do. The larger responsibility where the expertise comes in and a lot of the funding needs is that conservation work, which is absolutely required or the artifact will be destroyed. And then of course, the end goal of all this is that it should be on display for the public. Over the years we did small recoveries of some of the personal items from the crew members that we found that were on the surface. So that was telling the story. But then, you know, we started realizing in the mid 90s that, you know, Monitor the iron vessel and saltwater starting to corrode and deteriorate. What they thought was an accelerated rate. So they said, what can we do to protect this heritage? Do we do nothing and we let it fall apart? Well, you can do that. Can you recover everything, the entire ship? Well, you can think about that too, but do you think of the exorbitant expense and maybe damaging. Well, you try to do good, but you've actually damaged more so by the wreck falling apart because you can't something happens. HOST: And taking away the wildlife. TANE CASSERLEY: Yeah. And you would take away that reef as well. So they, I think feel, I feel very, that they made the right decision smartly to go after targeted pieces. So they said, what made the Monitor special? Well, it's that turret, right? That first rotating gun turret. That's what made it special. That's what it's known for. There's other aspects, but that's what, but you imagine in your head. Just so happens that the Monitor's entire drive train as the vessel sank was on top of the turret. Well, that's also very iconic and all of these things happen to be designed and built by John Erickson, the Monitor's designer. Well, the Navy working alongside NOAA, said, what can we do? And I said, well, why don't we target those mechanical spaces, the drive train and the turret. HOST: What's a drive train? TANE CASSERLEY: That's a good question. The drive train, we think about like a car, right? It's the engine. It's going to be the propeller shaft and the propeller itself. Basically, those things that make the ship go. All of that was on top of the turrets. Because as the vessel sank, the turret falls off, flips upside down, the rest of the Monitor flips upside down and falls on top. And it just so happened that it was scooted back a little bit where that engine space is now over that turret on the sea floor. It made sense. Let's focus on that. But also leave those crew areas intact where the officers and crew lived and worked is still totally intact on the sea floor and we managed to protect it because you know, it is a gravesite. So we focused on these mechanical technological parts. And that's what we worked with the U.S. Navy with from 1998 to 2002, where we conducted literally the largest archaeological metals recovery in history, bringing up over 200 tons of the pieces and parts of the shipwreck. And now here at the Mariners’ Museum and Park is the largest metals conservation marine project in the world, all dedicated to Monitor. HOST: Is the recovery of items complete or is it ongoing? TANE CASSERLEY: We look at the recovery items of the shipwreck now as on pause. We've got a lot of material to go through still. So the turret was brought up, for example, in 2002, that's still undergoing conservation to hear we are in 2026. So we really need to get through what we have now, I think, and get that on display. You know, there's a cost to that too that we have to think about, how do we do this? Again, never been done before, just like Monitor, something like never been built before. Something of this scale as a marine metal conservation project has never been put on display before. So it's exciting. But I like to think once we get through all of that, then we can rethink what's next, right? And that's always a great thing with Monitor. Ask the question, what's next? Because there always will be something next. HOST: Thank you so much for telling me the entire history of the Monitor. It's so fascinating. And it's funny that you say what's next, because in our next podcast, we'll be discussing just that. HOST: This has been Allison Burrell with the NOAA Ocean Podcast. Thanks to Tane Casserley for giving us a deep dive into the history of the USS Monitor. In Part 2 we’ll return to the Monitor National Marine Sanctuary to cover a new imaging technology that strives to capture the most detailed scan of the USS Monitor to date. What has happened to the USS Monitor over the last 140 years, what have we learned from the wreck, and what is being done to preserve its most treasured parts? Be sure to check out all our episodes through the National Ocean Service website or wherever you get your podcasts. Thanks for listening. Let’s keep making waves.
